title: The Workplace is Changing

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Research suggests that a business's success depends partly on its ability to accept new ideas about the workplace. Newspaper columnist Jennifer Dziura asks whether it even makes sense any more to talk about ‘a career’ when our professional and personal lives are so blended? It’s a good question according to a Canterbury University study, which suggests an increasing number of workers are rejecting the old notion of a single, permanent job, instead choosing a number of often temporary roles for different organisations, perhaps simultaneously. But how easy is it to actually do? Fallon Ashworth has been experimenting for the last six years, working as marketing manager for a grocery importer and running her own wedding planning company in her spare time. Says Ashworth, ‘I have to start early or finish late often, so I can take time off to organise weddings. Balancing everything can be tough, but I've just chipped away slowly.’ However, she says she feels better for having taken on the challenge.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Another interesting innovation is allowing company staff to put their inner entrepreneurial spirit to use without traditional corporate structures slowing them down. One way of doing this is for businesses to bring together a group of hand-picked staff members who are given responsibility for one particular task — perhaps developing a new product or rethinking their brand. Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Brett O'Riley is one who has set up such a group and says, ‘The result they achieved was phenomenal — employee engagement is high, and we have a unified team who own their own vision.’ Business academic Paddy Miller adds that encouraging such groups to form avoids the situation where ‘great people take their passion and ideas elsewhere because their organisations cannot embrace innovation.’

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: With more and more employees having the choice to work from the comfort and convenience of their own home, offices need to look pretty good to attract great people. As a result, employers are starting to think smart about space. Architect Tim Hooson says the way the office is laid out should support collaboration among the workforce, with specific areas and spaces set up for each activity they might want to do. Of course, this trend comes with its own acronym: ‘ABW’ or Activity Based Working. Yvette Grierson is one bank employee who's tried ABW and puts it this way: ‘At first I thought I'd miss having my “own” space — but it’s fabulous. We have areas for computer work, quieter places for phone calls, meeting spaces — and wherever you log in, your computer brings up your last session. No down time.”

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Another trend is apparent in an increasing number of workplaces, A recent Buck Consultants study of New Zealand and Australian workplaces reports 37% have what's being called a ‘wellness programme’, and Brad Norris of Synergy Health in Christchurch believes that this will just continue to increase. He's helped guide wellness programmes for large New Zealand companies, including banks, insurers and energy producers. Programmes are tailored to client needs, but can include anything from nutrition advice, to keeping fit and sleeping well. Norris says the benefits include attracting talent, reducing sickness absences, improving productivity and morale, and avoiding workplace accidents.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: An idea that’s already established in smaller companies, from California's Silicon Valley to Wellington in New Zealand, is for managers to sit down with their employees and say, ‘So what role do you think you'd be good at?’ Now this philosophy is spreading to larger corporates, encouraged along by recruitment agencies like Frog, whose CEO Jane Kennelly says, ‘It makes sense to work with who you have — they could be anywhere, in your marketing department, in human resources... people who are itching to make a difference and create something.’ These so-called ‘intrapreneurs’ are the perfect hire, according to Kennelly, because they are inherently entrepreneurial with big ideas, but don’t want the risk of starting their own business, so let them create their own role,

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: But perhaps the most significant new trend is in workplace dynamics. Statistics New Zealand estimates that over the next ten years, the percentage of the population over 65 will have increased dramatically. This means that any workplace will be made up of people far more varied in terms of their ages compared to any previous time. Frog’s Jane Kennelly says that smart workplaces can deal with this potential problem by transferring knowledge between the generations, and the best way to do this is to select certain employees to be mentors within an organisation. Meanwhile, a 2014 survey found that women’s participation in the workforce was 63.4%. That's partly because more mothers are returning to work after having children, but it’s not always easy for them. Some businesses like JP Morgan Chase are overcoming this issue with re-integration programmes targeted specifically at this group. Then there’s a separate development. In 2014 in Auckland there were over 200 different ethnic communities represented in the workforce. This can be an advantage for many businesses, exporters in particular. Says CEO Molly Harris, ‘Having staff with first-hand knowledge of some of the countries we work within enhances our operations.’ She acknowledges, however, that cultural mix can mean that communication is a challenge in some work environments. It’s just one more issue that companies must tackle moving forwards.
